title: I am looking for more directors like Terrence Malick and Werner Herzog that are fascinated by animal life and nature

commenti.body: [removed]

Maybe Joe Weerasethakul? Not the central thematic focus of his films but they're chock-full of that sort of imagery. The films of Terrence Davies also remind me of Malick's languid storytelling style (funny that they share a name).
Also Shohei Imamura

Jean-Jacques Annaud: Quest for Fire, The Bear, Two Brothers

Jamie Uys: Animals Are Beautiful People, The Gods Must Be Crazy

Godfrey Reggio: Koyaanisqatsi, Powaqqatsi, Anima Mundi

Ron Fricke: Chronos, Baraka, Samsara

Jacques Perrin: Winged Migration, Seasons (2015)

A lot of those are documentaries, but they go beyond what documentaries normally do.

Lav Diaz. So many of his frames are basically composed around nature, the presence of humans practically feeling like an intrusion to the space. I've been to his sets, and he's the type of director that won't cut if an animal enters the frame. The actors are the ones who have to work around it, because they're the ones who don't belong in this rustic scenario.

Also, have you seen Jerzy Skolimowski's Eo? That's a movie told from the perspective of a donkey.

I don’t have a filmmaker to recommend, but the movie Nope seems to fit your criteria.   Animals, their nature and our relationship to them are explored on three different levels.  I don’t want to say any more because of spoilers, but it is a great movie.

I just watched American Honey (2016) the other day. I don't know the director's other work at all, but I was struck by all the animal and nature imagery in the film. It left me wondering what the significance was. The main character helps a bee get out of the house at one point and there's a squirrel that basically lives in this one dude's hair. It's all very fascinating. A real gem of a film too that somehow slipped under the radar for me. Highly recommend!

A bunch of good suggestions already, and I'd add Franco Piavoli to the list. Nature and life cycles feature quite a bit in his documentaries and fiction films.

I agree with your description. Herzog is probably more interested in the chaos and brutality than Malick, yes. Though with a film like *Badlands* you can see humanity's use/abuse of animals coming through. There's a shot of Holly throwing her fish away, the dead dog among the garbage, her father shooting her own pet dog, the dead cows in the stockyard etc. I think there's a cold indifference here that Malick is highlighting, and he's tying it in with the meaningless death in the central Kit/Holly narrative.

Debra Granik is definitely fascinated by the relationship between humans and animals - it's not her central focus (though it's most prevalent in her short film Snake Feed) but it was one of the main things that stood out to me when I was watching her work. Animals are featured in all her movies and they're something she likes to highlight as part of her interest in environments.

Add Akira Kurosawa to the list.

* Tomm Moore: Wolfwalkers (2020), Song of the Sea (2014), Secret of Kells (2009)
* Hayao Miyazaki: Princess Mononoke (1997), Nausicaä (1984), The Boy and the Heron (2023)

Both are very interested in the mythology and legends, as well as in the (dis)harmony that human society consciously and unconsciously creates between themself as part as well as as some sort of tamer of nature. 

* Béla Tarr: The Turin Horse (2011), Werckmeister Harmonies (2000)
* Robert Eggers: The Northman (2022), The Lighthouse (2019), The Witch (2015), though in all cases almost exclusively as metaphorical means
* Martin Rosen: The Plague Dogs (1982), Watership Down (1978), quite obvious
* Kim Ki-duk: The Net (2016), The Isle (2000), same as Eggers only with exclusively fish & lakes
* Alejandro Jodorowsky: The Holy Mountain (1973), El Topo (1970), tho a lot of what he does is just to shock people (I know he's held in high esteem, but not by me lol)

Very interesting observation by the way. All I can do is stretch lol.

Miyazaki for sure, and the fact that it's animated just makes it even more impressive as it's something that so much work went into. One of my favourite scenes is the bus stop in My Neighbour Totoro and there's a little frog there who gets his own time to shine. It doesn't further the plot at all, it's just there because he wanted it to be. Lots of his films including MNT, Nausicaa, Ponyo and Princess Mononoke deal with elements of nature/wildlife and their interaction with the human world. Also worth thinking about how awareness of Shinto beliefs might impact his work (he is not Shinto but has talked about how much he respects it and you can definitely see the influence in his work).

Ciro Guerra's *Embrace of the Serpent* is very much in this vein. The stark beauty of the Amazon complements its ideas about spirituality and culture. Features a Tapir.

Alejandro Landes's *Monos* is brutal and raw, very political, but also cannot be told without its grounding in the Amazon. Features a cow.

Tarr was the first one who came to mind for me, when I saw him at a Q&A last summer he talked about his disdain for National Geographic-type documentaries that try to cut nature down into essentially narrative filmmaking with clean cut stories, good guys and bad guys, fast pacing, etc., and how his goal in his films is to portray nature the way it really is. Not just animal and plant life, but say, a cement wall. Just finding the nature in everything and not trying to understand it in strictly human terms.
